title: G1 review katas: reviewing a patch
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 review-katas row): scope = the 52 G1 patch katas on content/paths/agentic.json (easy, medium, hard); sources = katas whose seeded defects teach the idea. The new rv2 C5 katas are appended when they land. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Review what the change does to behaviour, not how it looks: a 'tidy-up' is a defect the moment it changes what a caller sees.
ideas.why: Style comments fill the review while the behaviour change slips through, often in exactly the patch that calls itself cosmetic.
ideas.prompt: A PR titled 'remove redundant return await' touches one line inside a try block of an authenticated route handler. The author says it is cosmetic. What do you check?
ideas.answer: Whether the behaviour is really the same. Inside try, returning the promise without awaiting it means a rejection is no longer caught by that catch, so an auth error can skip the handler's error mapping and reach the client as a different status. Ask for a test that sends an unauthorised request and asserts the HTTP status it gets back.

ideas.idea: A finding is complete with four parts: where (file and line), the input or scenario that breaks it, the consequence for a user, and the fix.
ideas.why: 'This looks wrong' gets argued away; a concrete scenario and consequence turn an opinion into a bug the author can reproduce.
ideas.prompt: You suspect a patch that looks up a library loan 'by book id alone' is wrong. Write the finding you would leave, not just the suspicion.
ideas.answer: Location: the lookup line. Scenario: a copy that was borrowed and returned before is borrowed again and now returned. Consequence: the lookup returns the oldest loan, already closed, so the return fails or closes the wrong record. Fix: also filter on the loan still being open, and add a test with a returned loan in history.

ideas.idea: Start with the changed lines and what they removed: most seeded and real defects sit in the patch, and the rest of the file only explains why.
ideas.why: Reviewers who read whole files first spend their time on old code and miss the one deleted condition the patch is really about.
ideas.prompt: A 40-line diff to a pricing module changes one comparison from inclusive to exclusive and reformats the rest. Where do you spend the first five minutes?
ideas.answer: On the changed comparison: list the boundary values it now handles differently (the exact maximum, a band where minimum equals maximum) and follow what happens when nothing matches. Only then read the surrounding code to see which checks depend on a match. The reformatted lines come last.

ideas.idea: Check that a test exercises the changed behaviour and would fail without the change; a green suite that never reaches the edited line proves nothing.
ideas.why: Suites stay green when a guard is deleted if no test ever sends the input the guard exists for.
ideas.prompt: A patch removes a 'redundant' second check in a repository lookup, and the full suite stays green. The author says the tests prove it is safe. What do you answer?
ideas.answer: Green only means no test sends an input that needs the check. Ask which test calls the lookup with an id from another site or tenant; if none does, the suite cannot tell. Write that test first: it should fail with the check removed. Here the check is object-level authorization, so the patch is a leak.

ideas.idea: Walk the same checklist over every patch: boundaries, null or missing data, the error path, concurrency, and who is allowed to do this.
ideas.why: Without a checklist you find the bug you were primed for and miss the race or the missing permission check next to it.
ideas.prompt: A patch lets admins approve their own purchase orders 'to save time', and also simplifies the approve write. Run your checklist and name what you find.
ideas.answer: Authorization: an admin approving their own order removes the separation of duties for the most powerful role. Concurrency: if the write no longer re-checks the pending status, two approvers clicking at once both succeed. Boundaries, missing data and the error path come next; two findings already justify blocking.

ideas.idea: Order findings by severity: data loss, security and money first, wrong results next, cosmetic last; say which ones block the merge.
ideas.why: A flat list puts a naming nit next to a refund bug, and the author fixes the easy ones first.
ideas.prompt: Your review of a refund patch has five findings: a misleading variable name, a status that contradicts the database, a rejected second partial refund, a missing log line and a typo. How do you present them?
ideas.answer: Lead with the blockers: legitimate partial refunds now rejected (money and customer impact), then the response that disagrees with what was stored. Mark both as merge blockers with their scenarios. The missing log line is a should-fix; the name and the typo are optional nits at the end, clearly labelled.

ideas.idea: Report only what is really wrong: a finding needs a breaking input, and a patch without one deserves an approval, not invented nits.
ideas.why: Padded reviews train authors to ignore you, and a reviewer who always finds something cannot be trusted when it matters.
ideas.prompt: You reviewed a small patch for ten minutes and found one real defect. You feel you should list a few more 'to be thorough'. What should the review contain?
ideas.answer: The one defect, with its scenario and consequence, and a clear statement of what you checked and found correct. Extra comments without a breaking input are noise; mark genuine style preferences as optional. If you had found nothing, the right review would say so and approve.
